title: Why Houses Became Unaffordable (And Who's Buying Them)
sources: NAR Existing-Home Sales, August 2026 (released Sept 10, 2026): median existing-home price $429,100 (+1.6% YoY, 38th straight monthly YoY gain); inventory 1.62M, 4.9 months' supply; individual investors/second-home buyers 15% of sales; all-cash 27%
U.S. Census Bureau, Income in the United States: 2025 (Sept 15, 2026): median household income $87,460

1995 comparison: NAR median existing-home price ≈ $110,500 (1995 annual); Census CPS ASEC Table H-5 median household income 1995 = $34,076 (current dollars). Ratio 110,500 ÷ 34,076 ≈ 3.2; 2026: 429,100 ÷ 87,460 ≈ 4.9
Freddie Mac PMMS, Sept 24, 2026: 30-year fixed 7.03% (year ago 6.30%); 1995 annual average ≈ 7.9%

Payment math (principal + interest, 20% down, 30 years): 1995 $88,400 at 7.93% ≈ $644/mo ≈ 23% of $2,840 monthly median income; 2026 $343,280 at 7.03% ≈ $2,291/mo ≈ 31% of $7,288 monthly median income. Down payment 20%: $22,100 (0.65 yr income) vs $85,820 (≈1 yr income)
FHFA National Mortgage Database via Redfin (Sept 29, 2025, Q2 2025 data): 52.5% of mortgaged homeowners have a rate below 4%, down from a record 65.1% in 2022
Up for Growth, Housing Underproduction in the U.S. 2025 (Nov 24, 2025): 3.78 million homes underproduced (2023 data); Freddie Mac estimate ≈ 3.7 million (2024)
NAHB (2021): regulation accounts for ≈ 23.8% of the price of a new single-family home
Institutional investors: GAO-24-106643 (2024) and Urban Institute: large investors (1,000+ homes) own roughly 3% of single-family rental homes nationally, but about one in four in metro Atlanta
NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers (Nov 2025): first-time buyer share record low 21%, median first-time buyer age record high 40 (29 in 1981)

beats.text: In nineteen ninety five, Dave's dad bought a house. One salary. Two kids. A yard. A dog named Biscuit.
Today, Dave and his partner both work full time. Two salaries. And they still can't afford a house.
Back then, a typical house cost about three years of income. Today, almost five years.
And it gets worse. The average first time buyer in America is now forty years old. A record.
So who is buying all the houses? Wall Street? Your neighbor? A raccoon in a suit?
Today: the price problem, the rate trap, the missing homes, the investors, and what Dave can actually do.
Let's start with a simple ruler. How many years of income does a house cost?
In nineteen ninety five, the typical American household earned about thirty four thousand dollars a year.
And the typical existing home cost about one hundred and ten thousand. That's about three point two years of income.
Now fast forward. The Census Bureau says median household income in twenty twenty five was eighty seven thousand dollars.
And in August twenty twenty six, the median home sold for four hundred and twenty nine thousand dollars. That's about four point nine years of income.
Think of it like a ladder. Incomes climbed a few steps. House prices took the elevator.
But the price is only half the story. Most people borrow. So the interest rate matters a lot.
Remember our mortgage video? A three hundred thousand dollar house can cost you seven hundred and twenty thousand, because of interest.
According to Freddie Mac, the average thirty year mortgage rate is now about seven percent. A year ago, it was six point three.
Dave's dad paid about eight percent. Sounds worse, right? But he borrowed way less money.
His monthly payment was about six hundred and fifty dollars. Less than a quarter of a typical income.
Dave's payment on today's median home? About two thousand three hundred dollars a month. Almost a third of a typical income. Before taxes and insurance.
And the down payment? For Dad, twenty percent was about eight months of income. For Dave, it's a whole year.
So why aren't there more houses for sale? Here's a weird one.
During the pandemic, mortgage rates dropped to around three percent. Millions of people locked in super cheap loans.
Today, about half of all homeowners with a mortgage still pay less than four percent.
Now imagine you're one of them. If you sell and buy another house, you swap your four percent loan for a seven percent loan. Your payment jumps.
So people stay put. Even when the kids move out. Even when the house is too big. Economists call it the lock in effect.
It's like golden handcuffs. Nice and shiny. But you can't leave. And fewer sellers means fewer homes for Dave.
But the biggest reason is simple. America didn't build enough homes.
After the two thousand eight crash, builders went bust. For about ten years, construction was way too slow.
Meanwhile, millennials grew up and wanted their own place. Lots of new households. Not enough new houses.
How big is the gap? Freddie Mac estimates about three point seven million homes. The group Up for Growth says about three point eight million.
Think of musical chairs. Ten people, eight chairs. When the music stops, people fight for chairs. And the chairs get very expensive.
So why not just build more houses? Well, it's harder than it looks.
First, the rules. In many cities, most land is zoned for single family homes only. No apartments. No townhouses. One big house per big lot.
Getting a permit can take months. Sometimes years. And neighbors often show up to meetings and say: build it, just not here.
The home builders' association estimates that regulations make up about twenty four percent of the price of a new home.
Then there's the stuff itself. Land, lumber, workers. All more expensive than they used to be.
Now, to be fair, some rules exist for good reasons. Safety. Traffic. Nature. That's a political question. Now you know the numbers.
Okay. The big question. Is Wall Street buying all the houses?
Most people think giant investors own most homes. Nope. Nationally, large investors with a thousand homes or more own only about three percent of single family rental homes.
But here's the twist. They're not spread out evenly. They bunched up in a few fast growing cities.
In the Atlanta area, large investors own roughly one in four single family rental homes. In some neighborhoods, they really do compete with families like Dave's.
And there's another group. Small investors. Regular people buying a second home or a rental. In August, they made up about fifteen percent of home sales.
So investors are a real problem in some places. But the national story is mostly the missing homes.
Put it all together, and you get this.
The National Association of Realtors says the typical first time buyer is now forty years old. A record high. In nineteen eighty one, it was twenty nine.
And first time buyers made up just twenty one percent of buyers. A record low.
Meanwhile, the people who already own homes have watched their prices rise. They win. The people trying to get in pay more.
Dave's dad got his first home at twenty eight. Dave is thirty four, and still renting. With a cat.
So what can Dave do? Education, not advice.
One. Renting is not throwing money away. Remember our mortgage video: if you might move in a few years, renting often makes more sense.
Two. Look at the whole monthly cost, not just the price. Taxes, insurance, repairs. The house is only the beginning.
Three. Check first time buyer programs. Many states and cities offer down payment help. Most people never ask.
Four. Compare lenders. Even a small difference in the rate can save thousands over the loan.
And five. Don't let the neighbors rush you. Buying a home is a huge decision. Take your time.
So let's recap.
One. A typical home went from about three years of income to almost five, and rates near seven percent make every payment bigger.
Two. Cheap old mortgages keep owners locked in, and America is short millions of homes.
Three. Big investors own a small share nationally, but a big share in some cities.
And that's a wrap. This was the last episode of Series Three.
Together, we found out why gas prices jump, whether A I is a bubble, how car loans trap people, and what a K shaped economy is.
Then how Starbucks, Apple and Amazon really make money, why subscriptions drain you, how banks profit from your savings, and today, housing.
Thirty videos. One much smarter Dave. So now, you decide. What should Dave explain next? Tell us in the comments. The best ideas go into Series Four.
And subscribe, so you don't miss it. It's free, and unlike houses, it will never cost five years of income.

youtube.hook: Why are houses so unaffordable? In 1995 a home cost ~3 years of income. Today it's almost 5. Here's what changed, and who's really buying. Dave's dad bought a house in 1995 on one salary. Dave and his partner can't, even with two. We compare home prices and incomes then and now (NAR, Census), explain why 7% mortgage rates hurt so much, how cheap pandemic mortgages created the lock-in effect, why America is short about 3.7 to 3.8 million homes, how zoning, permits and building costs slow construction, how much Wall Street investors really own (small nationally, big in Atlanta), and why the typical first-time buyer is now 40. This is the final episode of Series 3.
